---
title: "Cloudflare Cron Control"
description: "Operate the immediate-notification timer and the default-off scheduled job catalog on Cloudflare."
---

## Immediate notifications

The five-minute immediate-notification recovery timer runs in the
`tuturuuu-cron-control` Cloudflare Worker. It first calls the private
`requeue_mail_push_batches` RPC, then checks for a pending batch whose
`delivery_mode` is `immediate`. It invokes the existing web delivery processor
only when such a batch exists. The web processor still applies the recipient,
workspace, and delivery rules and atomically claims each pending batch. The
Worker sends an explicit empty JSON object and user agent to the web processor.
The web proxy requires a nonempty user agent for API traffic, and the JSON body
keeps the POST request unambiguous across Cloudflare and Vercel. The
matching entry is removed from `apps/web/vercel.json`; the authenticated web
cron route remains available for manual recovery. Other cron schedules remain
on Vercel until their own processors have safe Cloudflare gates or ports.

Production CI installs `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` on the Worker
from `PRODUCTION_SUPABASE_URL` and `PRODUCTION_SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY` repository
secrets. A separate `CRON_CONTROL_DELIVERY_TOKEN` repository secret is
installed on the Worker and in the web app's production environment to
authorize the delivery request. CI uses `COLAB_CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN` to deploy.
The Supabase secret key goes only in the `apikey` header for database calls.
Never add either credential to `cloudflare.config.ts` or logs.

Check the Worker `/health` endpoint and deployment marker after production
sync. Verify an idle schedule skips the Vercel call, then queue a test
immediate batch and confirm one delivery and a terminal batch status. Review
Cloudflare logs for RPC or delivery errors. During the brief rollout overlap,
both schedulers may run; the processor's pending-to-processing claim prevents
duplicate delivery. To roll back, restore the Vercel cron entry and remove the
Cloudflare trigger in a reviewed deployment.

An `Immediate batch delivery failed: 400` log may mean the web proxy rejected
the request before the processor ran. Check the proxy response source and the
Worker user agent, body, and content type. A `401` points to the web and Worker
delivery tokens being out of sync.

## Scheduled job catalog

Cron Control also owns the schedule for every legacy Vercel Cron job and the
`fetch-exchange-rates` pg_net job (`src/jobs.ts`). Each job calls the **existing
authenticated processor** over its current contract: the same route and method,
`Authorization: Bearer <that project's CRON_SECRET>`, the Cron Control user agent,
manual redirects and a per-job deadline. The processor keeps its own claims,
consent and idempotency rules. Cadences match the live legacy owner, not the stale
source catalogs. See the [background work inventory](/build/devops/background-work-inventory).

**Every job defaults off.** A job runs only when its id is listed in the
`CRON_CONTROL_ENABLED_JOBS` Worker var, so enabling one
is a reviewed configuration change. Production selects only database history
retention; legacy jobs remain disabled. While a job is off its tick performs no
storage or network work. Each enabled legacy HTTP job also needs its target
origin var and secret:

| Target | Origin var | Secret |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web | `WEB_ORIGIN` | `CRON_SECRET_WEB` |
| Infrastructure (also the Calendar gateway) | `INFRASTRUCTURE_ORIGIN` | `CRON_SECRET_INFRASTRUCTURE` |
| Inventory | `INVENTORY_ORIGIN` | `CRON_SECRET_INVENTORY` |
| Pay | `PAY_ORIGIN` | `CRON_SECRET_PAY` |
| Tasks | `TASKS_ORIGIN` | `CRON_SECRET_TASKS` |

Each secret holds the value the target project already uses for `CRON_SECRET`.
These legacy processor secrets are not in `secrets.required`,
and the production workflow does not install them yet. Installing them is a
separate reviewed workflow change or an operator `wrangler secret put`. An enabled
job whose secret or https origin is missing logs `Cron Control job misconfigured`
and does nothing.

A job with a Worker port (currently `inventory-checkout-expiry`) runs that port
instead of its Next route only when its id is also listed in
`CRON_CONTROL_WORKER_PROCESSORS`, which is empty by default. See
[processor migration](/build/devops/cloudflare-processor-migration).

### Ledger, claims and stop fence

The `CronLedger` SQLite Durable Object (one instance) stores per-job state:
last slot, lease expiry, generation, run count, consecutive failures and stop
state. It has no alarms, so only Cron Triggers start work.

- **Slot claim.** A tick claims `jobId` plus the scheduled minute. A duplicate or
  late delivery of the same or an older slot is refused, including after a Durable
  Object restart. A new slot is skipped while the previous run's lease is active.
- **Bounded work.** At most four processor calls run at once per tick. Claim-fenced
  and idempotent jobs retry once, after two seconds, and only for a network error,
  502 or 503. Processor errors, redirects and deadlines are never retried; a
  deadline is recorded as an unknown outcome. Handover jobs never retry.
- **Outcomes.** A 2xx needs a complete JSON object summary within 64 KiB.
  `ok: false` is failed; malformed, truncated, unreadable or oversized summaries
  are unknown and consume the failure budget without a retry. An absent `ok`
  field preserves existing JSON-object processor contracts. Bytes exceeding the
  remaining cap are rejected before retaining the chunk. Calendar provider sync
  also reports `degraded` for a valid `ok: true` response whose sampled provider
  accounts all failed transiently. This outcome applies only to
  `calendar-provider-sync`; other jobs ignore the Calendar degradation fields.
  `lastOutcome: degraded` survives a ledger restart and is visible in
  `GET /control/jobs`, while `lastCompletedAt` retains the last `ok` completion.
- **Failure budget.** Five consecutive failed or unknown slots stop the job
  (`failure-budget-exhausted`). A run terminated before it completes leaves an
  expired lease; the next claim charges it as unknown before admitting a
  replacement, so repeated terminations exhaust the budget too. The counter
  survives restarts and resets on an `ok` run, a nonfatal Calendar `degraded`
  run, or operator resume. Degradation does not spend the fatal budget or advance
  the timestamp of the last `ok` completion. Settled
  claims reject late completions, including after reconciliation exhausts the
  budget; late success cannot overwrite the unknown outcome. The dispatch and
  ledger unit regressions cover these cases across a simulated restart.
- **Operator stop.** `POST /control/jobs/<id>/stop` and `/resume`, plus
  `GET /control/jobs`, require `Authorization: Bearer <CRON_CONTROL_OPERATOR_TOKEN>`
  (32 characters or more); otherwise every control path returns the same 404 as an
  unknown route. A stop is checked before every claim and before a retry. Resume
  starts a new generation, so completions and retries from before the stop are
  ignored. Resume never enables a job; removing the id from
  `CRON_CONTROL_ENABLED_JOBS` is the deploy-time stop.
- **Fail closed.** If the ledger is unavailable, the job is skipped before its
  processor is called. A lost completion leaves the lease to expire and is then
  charged as unknown.

### Production operator token

Provision the independent stop control before enabling a production job. Ops
keeps the token on the M4 at
`~/.config/tuturuuu-ops/cron-control-operator.token` with mode `600` in a private
directory. Generate it directly into that file; never print it or pass its value
as a command argument. Create it once, retain it for incident response, and
coordinate any later rotation with the production deployment owner.

Upload that file with the repository's Wrangler `secret put
CRON_CONTROL_OPERATOR_TOKEN`, targeting `tuturuuu-cron-control` in account
`e8912e2867beecc673d171907bf09649`, with the file as standard input. Store the
same file using `gh secret set CRON_CONTROL_OPERATOR_TOKEN --env
cron-control-production --repo tutur3u/platform` with standard input. The normal
production workflow requires this secret and includes it in its private
`--secrets-file`, preserving the stop control on later publications.

Verify `GET /control/jobs` on
`https://tuturuuu-cron-control.tuturuuu-e89.workers.dev` returns `200` with
the token and `404` without it. Keep credentials in a child environment or
standard input, never a literal header in shell arguments. Before retention is
published, the authenticated job list must show no enabled jobs. The immediate
rollback is an authenticated `POST
/control/jobs/database-cron-history-retention/stop`; then remove the enabled id
through the reviewed configuration/deployment path. A bounded SQL batch already
running may finish after Stop.

### Cost envelope

Ticks fire whether or not jobs are enabled: about 2,020 Worker invocations a day
across the nine triggers, each a configuration check with no I/O while jobs are off.
An enabled job adds two Durable Object requests per slot (claim and completion),
each reading one row and writing at most one, plus one processor request (two
with a retry). With all 14 jobs enabled that is about 5,800 Durable Object
requests and writes a day. A persistently failing job makes at most five
processor calls before it stops, then one read-only claim per later tick.
These are request counts, not billed usage; the processors' own database,
provider and email work is unchanged. Moving a schedule does not reduce the
target project's function invocations; moving its processor does.

### First ledger publication

Production still runs the five-minute, `WEB_ORIGIN`-only Worker. The parity
baseline (`scripts/ci/fixtures/cf-worker-parity/cron-control.json`) records that
live identity as `previousIdentity` and the nine triggers, origin and stop-fence
vars and `CRON_LEDGER` binding as `identity`, under transition `CRON-LEDGER-1`.
The settings preflight admits the move only from that exact live state; see the
[settings transition rule](/build/development-tools/cf-cli-wrangler-parity#production-cutover-checklist).
Jobs and Worker processors stay off, so the change adds only the configuration-check
ticks counted above.

`cf deploy --prebuilt --no-provision` creates the `CronLedger` namespace itself:
cf 1.0.0-beta.20 sends a non-empty `exports` declaration in the script upload
instead of migration tags, and `--no-provision` only skips KV, D1, R2, queue,
AI Search, agent memory, dispatch namespace and Flagship provisioning. This first
`exports` publication on an existing script is unrehearsed; if the upload is
rejected, the publication step fails and `after` never runs. After promotion, check
`/health` and, where the operator token is installed, the ledger-backed
`GET /control/jobs`. Then remove the transition so later deployments return to the
unchanged-settings rule.

### Per-job cutover

Never run both owners unfenced, and never enable a job in production as a side
effect of another change.

1. Confirm the job's legacy owner, live cadence and last successful run, and that
   the target secret and origin are installed.
2. **Claim-fenced or idempotent jobs:** add the id to `CRON_CONTROL_ENABLED_JOBS`
   in its own reviewed change. After production sync, verify one Cloudflare slot:
   `GET /control/jobs` shows `lastOutcome: ok`, the processor logs one authenticated
   call and the domain state reached a terminal result. Overlap with the legacy
   owner is fenced by the processor's claim or convergence.
3. **Handover jobs** (`calendar-smart-schedule`, `web-deadline-reminders`,
   `infrastructure-docker-recovery-alerts`): remove the legacy entry first, confirm
   its last run, then enable the Cloudflare job and verify one slot.
4. Remove the legacy entry (`vercel.json` cron, or a new migration calling
   `cron.unschedule('fetch-exchange-rates')`) in a separate reviewed change, along
   with its cron-catalog entry. Then delete the matching entries from the
   [ownership guard](/build/devops/cloudflare-backend-ownership) allowlist.
5. Roll back by stopping the job through the control endpoint, removing its id,
   and restoring the legacy entry. Do not replay missed slots blindly: each
   processor recovers from its own durable state.

Recommended order: `tasks-cleanup-media`, `pay-products`,
`finance-exchange-rates`, `infrastructure-sync-trust-cache`,
`calendar-provider-sync`, the claim-fenced Web jobs, `inventory-checkout-expiry`,
the handover jobs, then `infrastructure-sample-resources` once its retirement
decision is made.

## Vite+ toolchain and validation

Cron Control owns a private Bun workspace with pinned Vite+ 1.1.0, the matching
Vite core alias, Cloudflare Vite plugin 1.63.1 and Wrangler 4.149.0. The owning
Wrangler supports the existing September 28 compatibility date; do not substitute
an older root runtime. The production Worker source, identity, five-minute trigger,
secret names and delivery protocol remain the same. `vite.config.ts` disables
remote bindings; the independent unit-test config does not start the Worker plugin.

From `apps/cron-control`, use Node 24 for `bun run lint`, `bun run test`,
`bun run type-check` and `node --test scripts/verify-worker-runtime.mjs`.
Use `ttr resources run -- <command>` for heavy local checks and a private home
`TMPDIR` if `/tmp` quota prevents runtime storage. Do not run release builds locally.
CI builds with `bun run build`, repeats the real local Worker HTTP checks using
`CRON_TEST_CONFIG=dist/worker/wrangler.json`, and checks emitted name/account,
compatibility date, trigger, vars and required secret names against the source.
CI retains `cron-control-worker-<full source SHA>`; the production-only job downloads
that tested artifact rather than rebuilding it. Keep explicit deployment approval
and exact-SHA production follow-through outside ordinary main integration.

Oxlint correctness rules are scoped to source/config files; Oxfmt configuration
and `format:check` are available for explicit parity review. Repository Biome
remains authoritative until the scope's formatting/rule/editor/generator gates
migrate together. No global formatting or framework migrator is needed.

The runtime fixture (`scripts/verify-worker-runtime.mjs`, on the shared cf Vite
harness) uses dummy credentials and checks the source config contract (every
legacy schedule, jobs default off, the `CronLedger` SQLite export), complete
health JSON, and rejection of HTTP invocation and unauthenticated control paths.
The harness accepts only declared secrets and the configured job list, so the
enabled-job contract (no work while disabled, one call per slot with the
expected auth, a slot claim that survives a ledger restart, operator
stop/resume and failure-budget exhaustion) is covered by the `ledger`,
`dispatch` and `control` unit tests rather than a runtime scheduled event. It
never dispatches the immediate-notification trigger and cannot certify database
recovery, web delivery, fanout, hosted schedules or total-spend bounds.
The existing four unit regressions preserve RPC-before-lookup ordering, idle skip,
authenticated delivery, redirect rejection and failure short-circuiting with
mocked downstream calls. A successful hosted schedule and terminal batch status,
persistent attempt/age limits, independent stop and alert evidence remain separate
acceptance work. The five-minute cadence and a delivery timeout are not total-spend caps.

Keep pool/worker defaults in the unit config and the package script as `vp test`.
Shared sharded CI appends its worker limit; validate `bun run test --maxWorkers=2`
under Node 24 to ensure the script accepts that override without duplicate options.

Vite+ 1.1.0 requires matching Vitest/coverage-v8 5.0.3. The root runner dependency,
root override and provider are pinned together; test the coverage override with
`bun run test --maxWorkers=2 --coverage` under Node 24. Ordinary tests alone do not
exercise the coverage version guard. Keep that guard enabled.

## Explicit immediate selection budget

After authentication, the web route reads at most 256 KiB in 4,096 stream chunks
before parsing JSON. Exceeding either bound returns HTTP 413, cancels the stream
and starts no database/provider work. The byte ceiling fits 100 maximum-length
IDs even when JSON-escaped. Malformed JSON retains HTTP 400. These request bounds do not
cap automatic delivery work or account spending. A ten-second total body-read
deadline returns HTTP 408 before database/provider work for stalled or slow
streams; receiving a chunk does not renew it. Monotonic elapsed checks before
and after each read, including end-of-stream, reject late reads even before the
timer callback runs. Cancellation is best effort and
cannot extend the deadline or replace an overflow/transport error.

Authenticated explicit batch selection accepts at most 100 `batch_ids`, with the
existing single-ID length bound applied to every ID. Oversized requests fail
validation before database access; split manual requests instead of silently
dropping IDs. Selection deduplicates IDs and uses one read capped at 100 rows.
Unrequested batches stay pending; selected batches retain complete delivery logs
and the existing atomic claims and ambiguous-send reconciliation fence.

Automatic recovery (empty body) retains complete pagination. Capping its oldest
window before root-workspace email filtering can repeatedly select ineligible
batches and starve later eligible deliveries. Further automatic selection bounds
require rollout-aware durable progress; do not silently truncate shared fetchAll
results or mark partial delivery logs as a completed batch.

The counted immediate-selection regressions cover explicit requests against
1,001 queued batches, duplicates, no progress, database failures and complete
automatic pagination. Request-budget and existing send-immediate route tests cover
validation and provider replay safeguards. The bound does not cap logs per batch,
devices, provider messages, automatic prefetch or recurring spend. Hosted delivery,
row accounting, durable cancellation and independent-stop evidence remain follow-up.

## Recovery request envelope

One idle recovery invocation still sends two database requests: stale-batch
requeue followed by the pending-batch lookup. A pending result adds one web delivery
request. At the configured five-minute cadence, 288 distinct invocations therefore
mean 576 database requests on an idle day, or 864 total requests when every lookup
finds work. These are request counts under those assumptions, not billed rows or a
hard daily cap; duplicate execution and downstream delivery fanout add work.

A failed requeue stops before lookup. A failed delivery occurs after both database
requests, so 24 independently retried calls perform 72 requests. The Worker has no
persistent retry reservation or recurring lease expiry. Its 180-second AbortSignal
covers web delivery; database recovery and lookup each use a 30-second
request deadline, as described below. The lookup asks for one row but consumes the complete JSON
response, so that query parameter does not prove a response-byte or storage-work cap.

Before bounding this path, verify actual database recovery rows and downstream
messages, reserve durable progress, bound every network phase and response read,
and preserve pending batch recovery across failures. Test duplicate schedules,
clock and stop/reschedule races rather than treating sequential helper calls as
hosted alarm evidence. Controlled fetch probes establish request ordering/counts;
real scheduled Worker, database, provider, authenticated independent-stop and alert
acceptance remain separate gates.

## Database request deadlines and redirects

Cron Control gives stale-batch recovery and pending-batch lookup separate
30-second AbortSignals. Lookup JSON consumption uses the same request signal;
headers arriving before the deadline do not restart it. A timeout propagates and
prevents subsequent lookup or delivery phases from starting. Recovery remains
before lookup, and the existing web-delivery deadline remains 180 seconds.

Database requests use manual redirects and reject non-success statuses, so the
Worker does not follow a redirect with its database credentials. A failed request
can have an unknown server-side outcome; preserve pending batches and the existing
idempotent database recovery contract. Do not add an immediate re-enqueue loop to
compensate for a timeout. The recurring schedule may retry later.

These per-request limits bound waiting when fetch honors cancellation, not the
number of recurring invocations, database rows, response bytes or provider messages.
They do not establish finite background jobs, authenticated independent Stop or a
spending cap. Worker unit tests cover stalled first/second phases, a stalled lookup
body and redirect short-circuiting with controlled fetch/abort behavior. Require
exact-head CI lint, types, tests and real emitted Worker checks; hosted scheduled
recovery and database/provider acceptance remain separate gates.

## Seven-day database cron history

The production configuration enables only `database-cron-history-retention`
in `CRON_CONTROL_ENABLED_JOBS` on the existing ten-minute trigger, after
`20261025210000` has been applied. The job catalog remains default-off; other
jobs stay disabled. Staging has no Cron Control Worker, so staging retention
is not applicable. This selection lives in
`apps/cron-control/cloudflare.config.ts` and its recorded parity identity;
publish it through the reviewed Cron Control production workflow. A source
merge alone does not prove live activation: read back the deployed binding
and verify the first three scheduled slots before accepting the rollout. It always
uses its Worker processor; it needs `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`,
not a web origin, web cron secret or `CRON_CONTROL_WORKER_PROCESSORS` entry.
No new pg_cron schedule or Next route is added.

Each slot calls `private.prune_cron_history(1000)` once. The RPC deletes at most
1,000 terminal `cron.job_run_details` rows and 1,000 completed
`public.workspace_cron_executions` rows whose end time is older than seven days.
Rows without an end time stay available for execution recovery. The pg_cron run-id primary key and managed-history end-time index, `SKIP LOCKED`, a ten-second statement timeout and a one-second lock
timeout bound each transaction. A backlog takes multiple slots; this is eventual
retention, not a promise that all expired rows disappear immediately. Do not
raise the batch size to catch up without reviewing database load.

The existing ledger deduplicates slots and preserves operator stop and failure
budgets across restarts. There is no in-slot retry or drain loop, including after
an ambiguous database outcome. At most 144 slots/day add 144 database requests,
432 ledger requests (claim, stop-fence check and completion) and 288,000 deleted rows/day across both tables.
A failed or unknown job stops after five slots. These are configured operation
bounds, not billing estimates. Use the authenticated stop endpoint before changing
or disabling maintenance; an in-flight SQL transaction can still finish its
bounded batch. Removing the enabled id prevents future claims.

The separate retired Docker log-drain database has a `cron_runs` table under its
existing summary-retention policy; it is outside this Supabase cleanup. Domain
audit history such as task and finance history is also excluded. No hosted row
counts are inferred from the disposable fixtures.

## Storage access audit retention

`database-storage-access-audit-retention` is a second default-off native
database maintenance job on the ten-minute trigger.
- It calls `private.prune_storage_access_events(1000)` once per slot, deleting
  at most 1,000 `private.storage_access_events` rows older than 90 days.
- The RPC uses the retention index, `SKIP LOCKED`, a ten-second statement
  timeout and a one-second lock timeout.
- It needs only `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_SECRET_KEY`. Enable it after the
  approved migration is applied; see
  [Storage access audit log](/build/devops/storage-access-audit).

Both retention jobs share `processors/maintenance-rpc.ts`:
- one request per slot, with no in-slot retry;
- a 1 KiB summary cap, integer counters up to the batch size, and manual
  redirects;
- the same ledger stop and failure budgets.

At most 144 slots/day add 144 database requests, 432 ledger requests and
144,000 deleted rows/day for this job.

## Meet transcript retention

`meet-transcript-retention` is a default-off native database job on the daily
`17 3 * * *` trigger. Unlike the single-request retention jobs, it runs up to 20
bounded batches per slot behind a database-owned fence and dry-run switch, with
at most three in-run retries. See
[Meet transcript retention](/build/devops/meet-transcript-retention).

The existing `refresh-posts-dashboard` pg_cron job remains pure database
maintenance at its ten-minute cadence. Its command must explicitly call
`private.refresh_posts_dashboard_view()` after the private-schema migration
removed the public helper. Test the stored `cron.job.command`, since calling the
private helper alone misses a stale scheduled command. The migration changes
only that command with `cron.alter_job`, retaining job id, cadence and active state.
Regression coverage: `supabase/tests/cron-history-retention.sql` and
`apps/cron-control/src/cron-history-retention.test.ts`.
